stem: Why is compromise of the CI/CD build pipeline MOST dangerous in a software ecosystem?

options.text: Malicious code can be injected into every build the pipeline produces
options.rationale: A compromised pipeline sits upstream of all builds, so attackers can poison every artifact it produces — a supply-chain catastrophe.

options.text: It only affects one developer's laptop
options.rationale: The pipeline builds for everyone; the impact is far broader than one laptop.

options.text: It makes builds run faster
options.rationale: Compromise is a security disaster, not a performance benefit.

options.text: It has no real impact
options.rationale: Pipeline compromise can distribute malware widely, a severe impact.

stem: A product includes many open-source libraries. Which control BEST manages the risk of vulnerable dependencies?

options.text: Software Composition Analysis (SCA) with an SBOM to track and patch components
options.rationale: SCA inventories dependencies and flags known vulnerabilities, and an SBOM enables rapid response when a component flaw is disclosed.

options.text: Assuming all open-source code is secure
options.rationale: Open-source components frequently contain vulnerabilities; blind trust is unsafe.

options.text: Removing all documentation of dependencies
options.rationale: Removing dependency records eliminates the visibility needed to manage them.

options.text: Using libraries without tracking versions
options.rationale: Untracked versions leave the product exposed when flaws are disclosed.

stem: A code review finds API keys hard-coded in the repository. What should be done FIRST?

options.text: Rotate the exposed secrets and move them into a secrets vault
options.rationale: Exposed secrets must be rotated (they may already be compromised) and relocated to a vault rather than remaining in source.

options.text: Leave them in the code for convenience
options.rationale: Hard-coded secrets in a repo are easily extracted and must be removed.

options.text: Publish them in the README
options.rationale: Publishing secrets makes the exposure worse.

options.text: Ignore it since the repo is internal
options.rationale: Internal repos are still accessible to many and can be leaked; secrets must be secured.

stem: To ensure no code reaches the main branch without peer review, which control is BEST?

options.text: Branch protection requiring approved code review before merge
options.rationale: Branch protection with mandatory review prevents unreviewed (and potentially malicious or flawed) code from merging.

options.text: Allowing anyone to push directly to main
options.rationale: Unrestricted direct pushes bypass review entirely.

options.text: Disabling version control
options.rationale: Removing version control eliminates review and history.

options.text: Deleting the review history
options.rationale: Deleting history reduces accountability and does not enforce review.

stem: A test account with production database credentials is compromised, exposing live data. Which control MOST directly would have prevented this?

options.text: Separating dev/test/prod environments with distinct least-privilege credentials
options.rationale: Proper environment separation ensures test credentials cannot access production data, containing the compromise.

options.text: Sharing one credential across all environments
options.rationale: Shared credentials are exactly what let the test compromise reach production.

options.text: Giving every environment full production access
options.rationale: Broad production access from non-prod environments increases risk.

options.text: Disabling all logging
options.rationale: Disabling logging reduces detection and does not separate environments.

stem: To detect tampering with a build artifact between the build server and deployment, which control is BEST?

options.text: Cryptographically sign artifacts and verify signatures before deployment
options.rationale: Signing build artifacts and verifying them at deploy time detects any tampering in transit or storage.

options.text: Rename the artifact to something random
options.rationale: Renaming does not detect content tampering.

options.text: Skip verification to deploy faster
options.rationale: Skipping verification allows tampered artifacts to be deployed.

options.text: Store the artifact on a public server
options.rationale: Public storage increases tampering exposure without detection.

stem: A developer can write code and single-handedly approve and push it straight to production. Which control MOST directly addresses this risk?

options.text: Separation of duties, so the author is not the sole approver of deployment
options.rationale: Separation of duties prevents a single person from both creating and releasing code, reducing the chance of unreviewed or malicious changes reaching production.

options.text: Giving the developer even more production access
options.rationale: More unilateral access worsens the problem.

options.text: Removing all approvals to speed delivery
options.rationale: Removing approvals eliminates the control that separation of duties provides.

options.text: Disabling code review
options.rationale: Disabling review removes oversight, increasing risk.

stem: To catch security issues early and automatically in development, where is it BEST to integrate SAST, dependency scanning, and secrets scanning?

options.text: Into the CI/CD pipeline so scans run automatically on each build
options.rationale: Integrating security tooling into the pipeline catches issues automatically and early, before code progresses.

options.text: Only manually, once a year
options.rationale: Annual manual scans miss most issues introduced between runs.

options.text: Never, to keep builds fast
options.rationale: Skipping scans trades security for speed and misses defects.

options.text: Only after a breach occurs
options.rationale: Reactive-only scanning leaves issues undetected until harm occurs.

stem: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) primarily helps an organization do which of the following?

options.text: Know which components are in its software so it can assess and patch vulnerabilities
options.rationale: An SBOM inventories components/dependencies, enabling rapid identification of exposure when a component flaw is disclosed.

options.text: Encrypt all network traffic
options.rationale: An SBOM is an inventory, not an encryption mechanism.

options.text: Serve as a firewall
options.rationale: An SBOM has no traffic-filtering function.

options.text: Replace the need for testing
options.rationale: An SBOM informs but does not replace security testing.

stem: Which practice MOST reduces the risk of unauthorized changes to source code?

options.text: Enforce least-privilege access to the repository with authentication and audit logging
options.rationale: Restricting who can access/modify the repo and logging changes reduces and attributes unauthorized modifications.

options.text: Make the repository publicly writable by anyone
options.rationale: Public write access invites unauthorized and malicious changes.

options.text: Share one admin account among all developers
options.rationale: Shared admin accounts destroy accountability and over-grant access.

options.text: Disable all logging on the repository
options.rationale: Disabling logging removes the ability to detect and attribute changes.

stem: Modern attackers increasingly target the software supply chain. Which statement MOST accurately reflects the resulting defensive priority?

options.text: Secure the entire build ecosystem (repos, pipeline, dependencies), not just the finished application
options.rationale: Because attacks target build systems and dependencies, defenses must cover the whole toolchain, not only the shipped app.

options.text: Only scan the final application and ignore the pipeline
options.rationale: Ignoring the pipeline/dependencies leaves the most-targeted areas unprotected.

options.text: Assume dependencies are always safe
options.rationale: Vulnerable/malicious dependencies are a primary supply-chain vector.

options.text: Security ends once code is written
options.rationale: Build, dependency, and deployment stages all require protection.

stem: Where is it BEST to store application credentials and API keys?

options.text: In a dedicated secrets manager/vault, retrieved at runtime
options.rationale: A secrets vault keeps credentials out of source, controls access, and enables rotation.

options.text: Hard-coded in the source repository
options.rationale: Hard-coded secrets are easily extracted from the repo.

options.text: In a public config file
options.rationale: Public config exposes the secrets to anyone.

options.text: Printed on a sticky note on the monitor
options.rationale: Physical exposure of secrets is grossly insecure.

stem: Which asset in the CI/CD ecosystem MOST warrants strong protection because its compromise enables signing malicious builds?

options.text: The pipeline's code-signing keys and deployment credentials
options.rationale: Signing keys and deploy credentials let an attacker produce trusted malicious builds, so they must be strongly protected (e.g., in an HSM).

options.text: The office Wi-Fi guest password
options.rationale: A guest Wi-Fi password does not enable signing builds.

options.text: The team's chat emoji set
options.rationale: Chat emojis are irrelevant to build integrity.

options.text: The cafeteria menu file
options.rationale: This has no bearing on build signing.

stem: Build agents currently run with broad administrative rights across many systems. What is the BEST hardening step?

options.text: Restrict build agents to least-privilege access scoped to what each build needs
options.rationale: Scoping build agents to minimal necessary permissions limits damage if an agent or pipeline is compromised.

options.text: Grant build agents domain admin everywhere
options.rationale: Over-privileged build agents massively increase blast radius on compromise.

options.text: Run all builds as the same shared root account
options.rationale: Shared root accounts destroy accountability and over-grant access.

options.text: Disable authentication on build agents
options.rationale: Removing authentication lets anyone control the agents.

stem: Beyond collaboration, version/configuration management MOST directly provides which security-relevant benefit?

options.text: A record of what changed and the ability to roll back to a known-good state
options.rationale: Version/config management tracks changes and enables rollback, supporting integrity and recovery from bad or malicious changes.

options.text: Automatic encryption of user data
options.rationale: Version control does not inherently encrypt user data.

options.text: Faster internet speeds
options.rationale: It has no effect on network speed.

options.text: Elimination of the need for testing
options.rationale: Version control complements, not replaces, testing.

stem: An attacker publishes a malicious package with the same name as an internal one to a public registry, hoping the build pulls it. Which control MOST directly mitigates this 'dependency confusion' risk?

options.text: Use trusted/private registries and pin/verify dependency sources and versions
options.rationale: Sourcing from controlled registries and pinning/verifying dependencies prevents the build from resolving to a malicious public package.

options.text: Always pull the newest package from any public source
options.rationale: Blindly pulling latest from public sources is exactly how dependency confusion succeeds.

options.text: Disable dependency management entirely
options.rationale: Removing dependency management is impractical and does not address source verification.

options.text: Ignore where packages come from
options.rationale: Not verifying package sources leaves the build vulnerable to substitution.

stem: What is the PRIMARY security benefit of mandatory peer code review before merging?

options.text: A second set of eyes can catch security flaws and malicious changes before they merge
options.rationale: Peer review surfaces vulnerabilities and unauthorized changes early, improving code security and accountability.

options.text: It makes the code compile faster
options.rationale: Review affects quality/security, not compile speed.

options.text: It removes the need for testing
options.rationale: Review complements, not replaces, testing.

options.text: It encrypts the repository
options.rationale: Code review does not encrypt the repo.

stem: To prove a deployed artifact truly came from the authorized pipeline and code, which practice is BEST?

options.text: Generate and verify signed provenance/attestation linking the artifact to its source and build
options.rationale: Signed build provenance/attestation cryptographically ties an artifact to its verified source and pipeline, defeating tampering and impersonation.

options.text: Trust any artifact that has a familiar file name
options.rationale: File names are trivially forged and prove nothing about origin.

options.text: Deploy whatever is on a shared drive
options.rationale: Unverified shared-drive artifacts could be tampered or malicious.

options.text: Skip verification to save time
options.rationale: Skipping verification defeats the goal of proving provenance.

stem: To prevent credentials from being committed to the repository in the first place, which control is BEST?

options.text: Automated secrets scanning (e.g., pre-commit hooks / pipeline scans) that block committed secrets
options.rationale: Secrets scanning detects and blocks credentials before or as they are committed, preventing exposure.

options.text: Encouraging developers to remember not to commit secrets
options.rationale: Relying on memory alone is unreliable; automation enforces it.

options.text: Making the repo public so mistakes are obvious
options.rationale: Public exposure worsens the impact of any committed secret.

options.text: Disabling commit history
options.rationale: Removing history hinders review and does not prevent secret commits.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST relevant to securing a software development ecosystem?

options.text: The desktop wallpaper on developers' machines
options.rationale: Wallpaper choice has no bearing on toolchain/pipeline/dependency security, making it least relevant.

options.text: Protecting CI/CD pipeline credentials
options.rationale: Pipeline credential protection is central to ecosystem security.

options.text: Managing dependency vulnerabilities with SCA
options.rationale: Dependency management is a core ecosystem control.

options.text: Enforcing code review and branch protection
options.rationale: Review/branch protection prevents unauthorized code changes, a key control.
